questionText: Reading Passage 3: The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

passage.title: The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
passage.subtitle: How intelligent machines are forcing society to confront difficult moral questions
passage.author: Dr. Helena Voss
passage.content:
Artificial intelligence has moved from the realm of science fiction into everyday life with remarkable speed. From recommendation algorithms that suggest what we should watch to autonomous vehicles that navigate city streets, AI systems now make decisions that affect millions of people daily. This rapid integration has raised urgent ethical questions that society is only beginning to address.

One of the most pressing concerns is bias. Machine learning systems learn from historical data, and if that data reflects existing prejudices, the system will reproduce and even amplify them. In 2018, researchers discovered that a facial recognition system used by a major technology company misidentified women of color at significantly higher rates than white men. The problem was not intentional malice but rather a training dataset that was overwhelmingly composed of images of light-skinned males. Such biases can have serious consequences when AI is used in hiring, lending, or criminal justice.

Transparency is another major challenge. Many modern AI systems, particularly deep neural networks, operate as black boxes. They produce outputs, but even their creators cannot fully explain how they arrived at a particular decision. This opacity becomes deeply problematic when an AI system denies someone a loan or flags them as a security risk. If the affected person has no way to understand or challenge the decision, basic principles of justice are compromised. Some researchers are working on explainable AI, but progress has been slow.

The question of accountability is equally thorny. When a self-driving car crashes, who is responsible? The manufacturer? The software developer? The passenger who failed to intervene? Legal frameworks were designed for human actors, and they struggle to assign liability when an algorithm makes a fatal error. Several countries have begun drafting new regulations, but there is little international consensus. The European Union has taken the lead with its Artificial Intelligence Act, which classifies AI systems by risk level and imposes strict requirements on high-risk applications.

Privacy concerns also loom large. AI systems thrive on data, and the more personal information they can access, the more accurately they can predict behavior. Companies collect vast troves of data on browsing habits, location, purchases, and even emotional states. While this data enables useful services, it also creates unprecedented opportunities for surveillance and manipulation. Authoritarian governments have already deployed AI-powered surveillance systems to monitor their citizens on a massive scale, raising fears of a digital panopticon.

Some philosophers argue that the real danger lies not in malicious AI but in our tendency to over-trust automated systems. Studies have shown that people tend to follow algorithmic recommendations even when they are wrong, a phenomenon known as automation bias. In healthcare, doctors may defer to an AI diagnostic tool rather than their own judgment, potentially missing nuances that a machine cannot detect. The solution, experts suggest, is not to abandon AI but to design systems that keep humans meaningfully involved in the loop.

Looking forward, the most profound ethical question may concern artificial general intelligence, a hypothetical system that matches or exceeds human capabilities across all domains. While such technology does not yet exist, many researchers believe it could arrive within decades. If it does, questions about rights, consciousness, and control will become unavoidable. For now, the challenge is to ensure that the AI systems we already have are fair, transparent, and accountable. The ethical decisions we make today will shape the relationship between humans and machines for generations to come.

questionText: Reading Passage 3: The Biology of Aging

passage.title: The Biology of Aging
passage.subtitle: How geroscience is redefining our understanding of growing old
passage.author: Dr. Marcus Chen
passage.content:
For most of human history, aging was viewed as an inevitable, irreversible process, a slow decline that all living things must eventually undergo. In recent decades, however, biologists have begun to reframe aging not as an unalterable fact of nature but as a biological process that can be studied, understood, and potentially slowed. This shift has given rise to a new field called geroscience, which seeks to understand the molecular mechanisms that drive the aging process.

At the cellular level, several hallmarks of aging have been identified. One of the most significant is telomere shortening. Telomeres are protective caps at the ends of chromosomes, and each time a cell divides, they become slightly shorter. When telomeres reach a critical length, the cell enters a state called senescence, in which it stops dividing but does not die. Senescent cells accumulate in tissues over time and secrete inflammatory molecules that can damage neighboring cells, contributing to age-related diseases such as arthritis, cardiovascular disease, and neurodegeneration.

Another key mechanism is mitochondrial dysfunction. Mitochondria are the energy-producing structures within cells, and they gradually lose efficiency as organisms age. This decline reduces the cell's ability to generate ATP, the molecular fuel that powers biological processes. Damaged mitochondria also produce reactive oxygen species, unstable molecules that can damage DNA, proteins, and lipids. For years, scientists believed that antioxidants could counteract this damage, but clinical trials have produced disappointing results, suggesting that the relationship between oxidative stress and aging is more complex than once thought.

The field was energized in 2006 when Japanese researcher Shinya Yamanaka discovered that introducing four specific proteins into adult cells could reprogram them into induced pluripotent stem cells, effectively reversing their cellular age. This groundbreaking work, which earned Yamanaka the Nobel Prize, demonstrated that cellular aging is not a one-way street. Since then, researchers have been exploring whether partial reprogramming could rejuvenate tissues in living animals without causing tumors, a major risk of full reprogramming.

One promising approach involves a class of drugs called senolytics, which selectively destroy senescent cells. In laboratory mice, clearing senescent cells has been shown to extend lifespan and improve physical function. Early human trials are now underway, though results remain preliminary. Another avenue of research focuses on caloric restriction. Studies in yeast, worms, flies, and mice have consistently shown that reducing calorie intake by roughly thirty percent can extend lifespan, apparently by activating cellular repair mechanisms that are normally suppressed when nutrients are abundant.

A drug called rapamycin, originally discovered on Easter Island, has generated particular excitement. Rapamycin inhibits a protein called mTOR, which acts as a nutrient sensor and promotes growth. By suppressing mTOR, rapamycin tricks cells into behaving as if they are starved, triggering repair and maintenance processes. In mice, rapamycin has been shown to extend lifespan by up to twenty-five percent, making it one of the most effective life-extending compounds known. However, its side effects, including immune suppression, make it unsuitable for widespread use in healthy people at present.

Skeptics caution that extending lifespan is not the same as extending healthspan, the period of life spent in good health. Simply living longer is of little value if those additional years are plagued by chronic disease. Most geroscientists argue that the primary goal should be to compress morbidity, reducing the period of illness at the end of life rather than merely postponing death. Whether the insights of geroscience will translate from laboratory organisms to humans remains an open question, but the pace of discovery has never been faster.

questions.paraphrasing: The target is to squeeze the duration of late-life sickness into a shorter window.

questionText: Reading Passage 3: The Economics of Climate Change

passage.title: The Economics of Climate Change
passage.subtitle: Why global warming is as much an economic problem as an environmental one
passage.author: Dr. Sofia Andersson
passage.content:
Climate change is often framed as an environmental problem, but economists increasingly argue that it is, at its core, an economic one. The burning of fossil fuels has driven unprecedented economic growth over the past two centuries, but it has also released vast quantities of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, creating costs that are only now becoming fully apparent. Understanding the economics of climate change requires grappling with market failures, intergenerational ethics, and the challenge of coordinating action among nearly two hundred nations.

The fundamental economic problem is that greenhouse gas emissions represent a classic externality. When a factory burns coal, it benefits from the cheap energy but does not pay for the damage caused by the carbon dioxide it releases. Because this cost is borne by society as a whole rather than by the polluter, the market produces more emissions than is socially optimal. The standard economic solution is to put a price on carbon, either through a carbon tax or a cap-and-trade system, so that polluters internalize the true cost of their actions.

Carbon taxes have been implemented in several countries, including Sweden, which introduced a carbon tax in 1991 and has since reduced its emissions by more than twenty-five percent while maintaining strong economic growth. However, carbon taxes face political resistance, partly because they can disproportionately affect low-income households who spend a larger share of their income on energy. Economists generally recommend returning the revenue to citizens as a dividend to address this concern, but such proposals have struggled to gain political traction.

Cap-and-trade systems offer an alternative approach. Under such a system, the government sets a cap on total emissions and distributes or auctions permits that allow companies to emit a certain amount. Companies that reduce their emissions can sell excess permits to those that need them, creating a market incentive for reduction. The European Union's Emissions Trading System, launched in 2005, is the world's largest, but it has been criticized for setting the cap too high in its early years, resulting in permit prices too low to drive meaningful change.

Estimating the economic cost of climate change is extraordinarily complex. The most widely used metric is the social cost of carbon, which represents the monetary value of damages caused by each additional ton of carbon dioxide emitted. Calculating this figure requires making assumptions about future economic growth, technological progress, and most controversially, the discount rate, which determines how much weight to give to future harms relative to present ones. A high discount rate implies that future damages matter little, justifying modest action today. A low discount rate suggests that we should invest heavily now to protect future generations. The choice of discount rate is not merely technical but deeply ethical.

The transition to a low-carbon economy also creates economic opportunities. The renewable energy sector is now one of the fastest-growing industries in the world, employing millions of people. Solar and wind power have become cost-competitive with fossil fuels in many regions, and battery technology is advancing rapidly. However, the transition will not be painless. Regions that depend on coal mining or oil extraction face significant economic disruption, and retraining workers for new industries is both expensive and logistically challenging.

International coordination remains the greatest obstacle. Because climate change is a global problem, a single country's reductions can be offset by another's increases. The 2015 Paris Agreement represented a landmark attempt to coordinate action, but its voluntary structure means that compliance cannot be enforced. Some economists have proposed border carbon adjustments, tariffs on goods from countries without adequate climate policies, to prevent companies from simply relocating emissions. Whether such mechanisms can be implemented without triggering trade wars remains to be seen, but the economic stakes of inaction grow higher with each passing year.

questionText: Reading Passage 3: The History of Pandemics

passage.title: The History of Pandemics
passage.subtitle: How infectious diseases have shaped human civilization
passage.author: Dr. James Okonkwo
passage.content:
Pandemics have shaped human history more profoundly than wars or revolutions, toppling empires, reshaping economies, and altering the course of civilizations. From the Plague of Athens to the COVID-19 outbreak, infectious diseases have periodically swept through populations with devastating consequences. The history of pandemics is not merely a chronicle of suffering but also a story of scientific discovery, social transformation, and the enduring human capacity for resilience.

The earliest recorded pandemic struck Athens in 430 BCE during the Peloponnesian War. The disease, which scholars believe may have been typhoid or typhus, killed an estimated quarter of the city's population and fatally weakened Athens in its struggle against Sparta. The historian Thucydides, who survived the disease himself, provided the first detailed account of a pandemic, noting that the overwhelming mortality caused a breakdown of social order as people abandoned their moral and religious obligations.

The most devastating pandemic in recorded history was the Black Death, which swept through Europe, Asia, and North Africa in the fourteenth century. Caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and transmitted by fleas on rats, the plague killed an estimated seventy-five to two hundred million people, reducing Europe's population by as much as half. The social consequences were enormous. With labor scarce, surviving workers demanded higher wages, contributing to the decline of the feudal system. The Catholic Church, unable to explain or halt the pestilence, suffered a crisis of authority from which it never fully recovered.

Centuries later, cholera pandemics swept across the globe in the nineteenth century. Originating in the Ganges delta, cholera spread along trade and military routes, reaching Europe and the Americas by the 1830s. The disease, which causes severe diarrhea and dehydration, could kill within hours. In London, the repeated cholera outbreaks prompted a physician named John Snow to investigate. In 1854, he mapped cholera cases in the Soho neighborhood and traced them to a single contaminated water pump. When the pump handle was removed, the outbreak subsided. Snow's work founded the field of epidemiology and demonstrated that diseases could spread through contaminated water rather than through bad air, as the prevailing miasma theory held.

The Spanish flu of 1918-1919 was the deadliest pandemic of the twentieth century, killing an estimated fifty to one hundred million people worldwide. Unlike most influenza strains, which disproportionately kill the elderly, the Spanish flu was particularly lethal to young adults, a pattern thought to result from an overreaction of the immune system known as a cytokine storm. The pandemic occurred during the final year of World War I, and wartime censorship initially suppressed news of the outbreak. The disease killed more people than the war itself, yet it faded quickly from public memory, leading some historians to call it the forgotten pandemic.

The development of vaccines in the twentieth century transformed humanity's ability to combat infectious disease. The eradication of smallpox in 1980, achieved through a global vaccination campaign, remains one of the greatest triumphs of public health. Yet the threat of pandemics persists. The emergence of HIV in the 1980s, the SARS outbreak of 2003, and the COVID-19 pandemic that began in 2019 have each exposed vulnerabilities in global health systems. COVID-19, which has killed millions, also demonstrated the power of rapid vaccine development, as mRNA vaccines were deployed within a year of the virus's identification, a process that previously would have taken a decade or more.

The history of pandemics offers sobering lessons. Each outbreak has revealed the same patterns: initial denial, delayed response, and disproportionate impact on the poor and marginalized. Yet each pandemic has also accelerated innovation in medicine, governance, and international cooperation. Whether humanity will be better prepared for the next pandemic remains an open question, but history suggests that the question is not if another will come but when.

questionText: Reading Passage 3: The Psychology of Addiction

passage.title: The Psychology of Addiction
passage.subtitle: Beyond moral failure: the science of compulsive behavior
passage.author: Dr. Rachel Brennan
passage.content:
Addiction has long been one of the most misunderstood phenomena in human psychology. For much of history, it was viewed as a moral failing, a sign of weak will or deficient character. People who could not stop drinking or gambling were seen as indulgent, irresponsible, and culpable for their own ruin. This moral model dominated public thinking for centuries and continues to influence social attitudes today, despite a century of scientific research that has thoroughly dismantled it. Modern psychology now understands addiction as a complex brain disorder shaped by neurobiology, environment, and experience, a condition that demands compassion and evidence-based treatment rather than condemnation.

At the center of the neurobiological account is the brain's reward system. When we engage in activities essential for survival, such as eating or social bonding, the brain releases dopamine, a neurotransmitter that produces feelings of pleasure and reinforcement. Addictive substances and behaviors hijack this system by triggering floods of dopamine far exceeding what natural rewards produce. Over time, the brain adapts by reducing its number of dopamine receptors, a process called downregulation. The result is tolerance, the need for increasing amounts of the substance to achieve the same effect, and anhedonia, a diminished capacity to enjoy ordinary pleasures.

However, the neurobiological model, while powerful, does not tell the whole story. If addiction were simply a matter of chemical hijacking, everyone who tried an addictive drug would become addicted. In reality, most people who use substances, even highly addictive ones like heroin or cocaine, do not develop addiction. This observation has led psychologists to search for additional factors that make certain individuals vulnerable. Research consistently shows that trauma, particularly adverse childhood experiences, is one of the strongest predictors of addiction. Individuals who experienced abuse, neglect, or household dysfunction in childhood are far more likely to develop addictive disorders later in life.

The environmental context also plays a crucial role. The classic Rat Park experiments of the 1970s challenged the prevailing view that drugs inevitably cause addiction. In these studies, rats housed in isolated, barren cages consumed morphine-laced water compulsively. But rats housed in an enriched environment with companions, toys, and space consumed far less, even when the drug was freely available. These findings suggested that addiction is not merely a pharmacological response but is deeply connected to social isolation and environmental deprivation, a perspective that has profound implications for how society approaches treatment.

Psychologists have also identified cognitive mechanisms that sustain addictive behavior. One of the most important is the phenomenon of craving, which is not simply a desire for pleasure but a conditioned response triggered by environmental cues. A person who smoked cigarettes in their car may feel an overwhelming urge to smoke every time they sit behind the wheel, even years after quitting. These conditioned responses are mediated by memory and learning circuits that persist long after the physical withdrawal has subsided, explaining why relapse is so common and why willpower alone is rarely sufficient.

The disease model of addiction has been enormously influential, but it has its critics. Some psychologists argue that calling addiction a disease risks stripping individuals of agency and oversimplifying a condition that involves choices, beliefs, and social context. They point out that many people recover from addiction without any treatment, and that the language of disease can be disempowering. Proponents of the disease model counter that it does not deny agency but rather reframes recovery as a process of managing a chronic condition, analogous to diabetes, where lifestyle choices matter but the underlying vulnerability persists.

Treatment approaches have evolved significantly. While early interventions relied on punishment and moral exhortation, contemporary treatment increasingly combines medication, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and social support. Medications such as methadone and buprenorphine can reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms, giving individuals the stability needed to address underlying psychological issues. Cognitive-behavioral therapy helps patients identify triggers, develop coping strategies, and reframe the thought patterns that sustain addictive behavior. Perhaps most importantly, peer support groups provide the social connection that the Rat Park experiments suggested is essential for recovery.

Ultimately, addiction sits at the intersection of biology, psychology, and society. It cannot be reduced to a single cause or cured by a single intervention. Understanding addiction requires acknowledging the suffering that often underlies it, the brain changes that perpetuate it, and the social conditions that either nourish or erode the capacity for recovery. As science continues to unravel the mechanisms of addiction, the most important shift may be not in the laboratory but in public attitudes, replacing stigma with understanding and punishment with treatment.
